---
title: "Part 2 – The claim and its estimand"
---
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Slides.** [Open the deck at this part](../../slides/housing-one-day-open-science.html#/part-2-the-claim-and-its-estimand){target="_blank"} in its own tab, or follow it on the [slides page](slides.qmd).
:::

Part 2 reads the paper, sets out what the five Multi100 analysts did with its claim, and argues that analysts who look as though they disagree are often answering different questions. It then gives you the tool for saying which question you are answering, the estimand statement, and you write one for the claim before lunch.

| Work through | What you do | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| Slides, Part 2 | The paper of the original authors (OAs): the question that it asks, the design, the email word for word, what came back for each of the six names, the four outcomes that were coded, and the claim as SCORE selected it, with its two ellipses. | 16 minutes |
| Slides, the five analysts | The five Multi100 analysts placed by their gaps in percentage points, then a table of what each of them did, with five different questions behind two different verdicts. | 6 minutes |
| Slides, the estimands run | Two studies set beside our five: the red-card estimates again as a single row, the four estimands that the twenty-nine teams were in fact pursuing, and the spread that collapses once the estimand is fixed. Then what under-specified research questions mean for the reading of many-analysts studies, and the steps from a theoretical to an empirical estimand that Lundberg and colleagues set out. | 16 minutes |
| Slides, the claim | The estimand statement, which everyone writes in chat, holds and sends together; the causal graph of the experiment; why comparing greetings among the replies conditions on a consequence of the name; and what changes when every delivered email is counted. | 14 minutes |
| Slides, the R tutorial | Optional, if the class wants it: R in one slide, reading and inspecting the data, the verbs that work on rows and columns, tables and tests, model formulas, a plot, causal graphs in R, and the error messages that you are most likely to meet. | 10 minutes |
| [Browser lab](../../cases/housing/lab.qmd#task-2-data) Task 2 | Count the emails that bounced, the replies, the replies with a greeting code and the greetings by name, for each name. Write the estimand statement with every bracket filled, saying which emails you count. If there is time, finish the causal graph in the [graph cell](../../cases/housing/lab.qmd#task-2-estimand-and-graph). Finish with two sentences: what a comparison among the replies conditions on, and what counting every delivered email changes. | 24 minutes |

**By the end of the part** you have the estimand behind the claim written in one sentence, and two sentences on why the choice of which emails to count changes the question. Both go into the preregistration block of Part 4.
